pageTitle: AWS threat signature managed rule groups for AWS Network Firewall
whatThePageStates: The page introduces the AWS managed rule groups that inspect for threat signatures in AWS Network Firewall, and says you can list them through the ListRuleGroups API. It then presents a single three-column table (Category | Rule name | Description and label) with 16 data rows. Each row names one threat category and gives two rule group names for it, one suffixed StrictOrder and one suffixed ActionOrder, so 16 categories yield 32 named rule groups. Prose before the table explains that the suffix must match the firewall policy's rule evaluation order, and states one limitation: Network Firewall currently supports only Suricata-compatible stateful managed rule groups. There is no Yes/No/Partial column, no Region column, and no statement anywhere that any category is unsupported.

features.featureName: AWS threat signature managed rule groups
features.statuses: 16 rows, all presence-only: 16 supported, 0 stated-not-supported, 0 partial; 16+0+0=16. There is no status column at all. Every row is an offered rule group, so its presence is the only affirmative signal; not-supported is never stated for any category, only ABSENT, so no negative coverage can be read off this page. The one explicit limitation in the prose ('Currently, Network Firewall supports only Suricata-compatible stateful managed rule groups') is a rule-engine constraint, not a per-category No, and it applies uniformly to all 16 rows.
features.scope: Rule evaluation order, with 2 values: StrictOrder and ActionOrder. Every one of the 16 categories is offered in both, which is why 16 categories produce 32 distinct rule group names (16x2=32). The page states the scope is a constraint of the firewall policy, not of the threat coverage: you may only attach a StrictOrder rule group to a strict-order policy. No Region scope, no pricing-tier scope, no account-type scope.
features.reasoning: The enumerated unit is the leftmost Category column, which is what defines the rows: Botnet, Botnet Web, Botnet Windows, Compromised, DoS, Emerging Threats, Exploits, FUP, Malware, Malware Coin Mining, Malware Mobile, Malware Web, Phishing, Scanners, Suspect, Web Attacks. This is a catalogue axis because AWS publishes the category list about its own rule groups; it is not an independently existing universe. The category, not the rule group name, is the unit of coverage claim: the StrictOrder and ActionOrder members of a pair carry identical signature coverage and differ only in which policy they may attach to, so counting rule group names would count the same protection twice. The alternative vocabulary axis managedRuleGroup would give 32 for the same table and is defensible on the page title alone, but it inflates the coverage measure 2x for a packaging detail. If a downstream measurement genuinely wants product SKUs rather than protections, the correct figure is 32 and it is stated here explicitly; the 16 vs 32 choice must be made deliberately, never by accident.

shouldNotExtract:
The 'See also' section, which is only the optional AWS Agent Toolkit skills-for-AI-coding-assistants boilerplate and the aws agent-toolkit search-skills command, is not coverage. Neither is the ListRuleGroups API link, the link to the rule evaluation order page (suricata-rule-evaluation-order.md), the HTML anchor tag under the H1, or the table's header and separator rows, which grep will return as two extra pipe-delimited lines and must not be counted as data. The long Description column is a special hazard: it contains dozens of embedded sub-labels separated by
markers, such as Attack Response, Exploit Kit, Current Events, ActiveX, FTP, ICMP, NetBIOS, RPC, ShellCode, SNMP, Telnet, TFTP, VOIP, SQL, JA3, Chat, User Agents, Web Client, Web Server, Web Specific Apps, Malware, Worm. These are prose descriptions of what a rule group detects, not separately selectable rule groups, and must not be harvested as axis values. Vendor and product names inside the descriptions, such as Nessus, Nikto, Metasploit, Apache, Tomcat, NGINX, IIS, CURL, WGET, Google Android, Apple iOS and Microsoft Windows, are examples and are not a coverage enumeration either.
coverageDimensions: REGION: the page gives nothing. It names no Region, no partition, and no availability table; any per-Region figure attributed to this page is fabricated. SERVICE: the page covers exactly one AWS service, AWS Network Firewall, and makes no statement about any other service; it is not a cross-service matrix and yields a service count of 1 at most, not 16. RESOURCE TYPE: the page gives nothing. It never names an AWS resource type, ARN shape, or CloudFormation type; the closest thing is the managed rule group itself, which is a Network Firewall catalogue object rather than a resource type in the inventory sense, and no per-resource-type coverage can be derived. The only real dimensions on this page are threat category (16) and rule evaluation order (2).
trap:
The single most likely misparse is counting rule group NAMES instead of rows and reporting 32 protections, because the Rule name cell holds two comma-separated names per row. StrictOrder and ActionOrder are the same coverage packaged for two policy modes, so 32 double-counts unless the measurement is explicitly about selectable rule group objects. Runners-up: (1) splitting the Description column on
and reporting roughly 20-plus extra sub-categories such as ActiveX, FTP, SNMP, JA3 and Web Server as if they were rule groups, which would inflate the count to 40 or more; (2) counting the markdown header and separator lines and reporting 18 rows; (3) inventing a No or unsupported status because the table has no status column, when in fact absence is not a claim and this page states nothing negative about any category; (4) treating the Suricata-only sentence as a per-row exclusion rather than a service-wide engine note; (5) attributing a Region count to a page that names no Region.
